entries.4d5bbedc8c4766c7dca4b89e7bf5bfe475017d20: <div sID="gen17422" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Jer.11" sID="Jer.11"/> <div eID="gen17422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17423" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17424" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. God by the prophet puts the people in mind of the covenant he had made with their fathers, and how much he had insisted upon it, as the condition of the covenant, that they should be obedient to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.1-Jer.11.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. He charges it upon them that they, in succession to their fathers, and in confederacy among themselves, had obstinately refused to obey him, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.8-Jer.11.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. III. He threatens to punish them with utter ruin for their disobedience, especially for their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.11">ver. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">13</reference>), and tells them that their idols should not save them (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">ver. 12</reference>), that their prophets should not pray for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">ver. 14</reference>); he also justifies his proceedings herein, they having brought all this mischief upon themselves by their own folly and wilfulness, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15-Jer.11.17">ver. 15-17</reference>. IV. Here is an account of a conspiracy formed against Jeremiah by his fellow-citizens, the men of Anathoth; God's discovery of it to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.18-Jer.11.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>), his prayer against them (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">ver. 20</reference>), and a prediction of God's judgments upon them for it, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21-Jer.11.23">ver. 21-23</reference>.
entries.77e8941dda2cac2cdbcccaefea25f9243d4c93c1: <div eID="gen17424" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17423" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Charges against Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17425" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear ye the words of this covenant, and speak unto the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem; <hi type="super">3</hi> And say thou unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel; Cursed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant, <hi type="super">4</hi> Which I commanded your fathers in the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Obey my voice, and do them, according to all which I command you: so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God: <hi type="super">5</hi> That I may perform the oath which I have sworn unto your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day. Then answered I, and said, So be it, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying, Hear ye the words of this covenant, and do them. <hi type="super">7</hi> For I earnestly protested unto your fathers in the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto this day, rising early and protesting, saying, Obey my voice. <hi type="super">8</hi> Yet they obeyed not, nor inclined their ear, but walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart: therefore I will bring upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded <hi type="italic">them</hi> to do; but they did <hi type="italic">them</hi> not. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them: the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers. <div eID="gen17425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17426" type="x-p"/> The prophet here, as prosecutor in God's name, draws up an indictment against the Jews for wilful disobedience to the commands of their rightful Sovereign. For the more solemn management of this charge, <div eID="gen17426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17427" type="x-p"/> I. He produces the commission he had to draw up the charge against them. He did not take pleasure in accusing the children of his people, but God commanded him to <hi type="italic">speak it to the men of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.1-Jer.11.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. In the original it is plural: <hi type="italic">Speak you this.</hi> For what he said to Jeremiah was the same that he gave in charge to all his servants the prophets. They none of them said any other than what Moses, in the law, had said; to that therefore they must refer themselves, and direct the people: "<hi type="italic">Hear the words of this covenant;</hi> turn to your Bibles, be judged by them." Jeremiah must now proclaim this in the cities <hi type="italic">of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem,</hi> that all may hear, for all are concerned. All the words of reproof and conviction which the prophets spoke were grounded upon the <hi type="italic">words of the covenant,</hi> and agreed with that; and therefore "<hi type="italic">hear these words,</hi> and understand by them upon what terms you stood with God at first; and then, by comparing yourselves with the covenant, you will soon be aware upon what terms you now stand with him." <div eID="gen17427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17428" type="x-p"/> II. He opens the charter upon which their state was founded and by which they held their privileges. They had forgotten the tenour of it, and lived as if they thought that the grant was absolute and that they might do what they pleased and yet have what God had promised, or as if they thought that the keeping up of the ceremonial observances was all that God required of them. He therefore shows them, with all possible plainness, that the thing God insisted upon was <hi type="italic">obedience,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">better than sacrifice.</hi> He said, <hi type="italic">Obey my voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.4">v. 4</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">v. 7</reference>. "Own God for your Master; give up yourselves to him as his subjects and servants; attend to all the declarations of his mind and will, and make conscience of complying with them. <hi type="italic">Do my commandments,</hi> not only in some things, but <hi type="italic">according to all which I command you;</hi> make conscience of moral duties especially, and rest not in those that are merely ritual; hear the words of the covenant, and do them." 1. This was the original contract between God and them, when he first formed them into a people. It was what he <hi type="italic">commanded their fathers</hi> when he first <hi type="italic">brought them forth out of the land of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.4">v. 4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">v. 7</reference>. He never intended to take them under his guidance and protection upon any other terms. This was what he required from them in gratitude for the great things he did for them when he brought them <hi type="italic">from the iron furnace.</hi> He redeemed them out of the service of the Egyptians, which was perfect slavery, that he might take them into his own service, which is perfect freedom, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. 2. This was not only laid before them then, but it was with the greatest importunity imaginable pressed upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">v. 7</reference>. God not only commanded it, but <hi type="italic">earnestly protested it to their fathers,</hi> when he brought them into covenant with himself. Moses inculcated it again and again, by precept upon precept and line upon line. 3. This was made the condition of the relation between them and God, which was so much their honour and privilege: "<hi type="italic">So shall you be my people and I will be your God;</hi> I will own you for mine, and you may call upon me as yours;" this intimates that, if they refused to obey, they could no longer claim the benefit of the relation. 4. It was upon these terms that the land of Canaan was given them for a possession: <hi type="italic">Obey my voice, that I may perform the oath sworn to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.5">v. 5</reference>. God was ready to fulfil the promise, but then they must fulfil the condition; if not, the promise is void, and it is just with God to turn them out of possession. Being brought in upon their good behaviour, they had no wrong done them if they were turned out upon their ill behaviour. Obedience was the rent reserved by the lease, with a power to re-enter for non-payment. 5. This obedience was not only made a condition of the blessing, but was required under the penalty of a curse. This is mentioned first here (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">v. 3</reference>), that they might, if possible, be awakened by the terrors of the Lord: <hi type="italic">Cursed be the man,</hi> though it were but a single person, <hi type="italic">that obeys not the words of this covenant,</hi> much more when it is the body of the nation that rebels. There are curses of the covenant as well as blessings: and Moses set before them not only <hi type="italic">life and good,</hi> but <hi type="italic">death and evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">Deut. xxx. 15</reference>), so that they had fair warning given them of the fatal consequences of disobedience. 6. Lest this covenant should be forgotten, and, because out of mind, should be thought out of date, God had from time to time called to them to remember it, and by his servants the prophets had made a continual claim of this rent, so that they could not plead, in excuse of their non-payment, that it had never been demanded; <hi type="italic">from the day when he brought them out of Egypt to this day</hi> (and that was nearly 1000 years) he had been, in one way or other, <hi type="italic">at sundry times and in divers manners,</hi> protesting to them the necessity of obedience. God keeps an account how long we have enjoyed the means of grace and how powerful those means have been, how often we have been not only spoken to, but protested to, concerning our duty. 7. This covenant was consented to (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then answered I, and said, So be it, O Lord!</hi> These are the words of the prophet, expressing either, (1.) His own consent to the covenant for himself, and his desire to have the benefit of it. God promised Canaan to the obedient: "Lord," says he, "I take thee at thy word, I will be obedient; let me have my inheritance in the land of promise, of which Canaan is a type." Or, (2.) His good will, and good wish, that his people might have the benefit of it. "<hi type="italic">Amen;</hi> Lord, let them still be kept in possession of this good land, and not turned out of it; make good the promise to them." Or, (3.) His people's consent to the covenant: "<hi type="italic">Then answered I,</hi> in the name of the people, <hi type="italic">So be it.</hi>" Taking it in this sense, it refers to the declared consent which the people gave to the covenant, not only to the precepts of it when they said, <hi type="italic">All that the Lord shall say unto us we will do and will be obedient,</hi> but to the penalties when they said <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to all the curses upon Mount Ebal. The more solemnly we have engaged ourselves to God the more reason we have to hope that the engagement will be perpetual; and yet here it did not prove so. <div eID="gen17428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17429" type="x-p"/> III. He charges them with breach of covenant, such a breach as amounted to a forfeiture of their charter, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.8">v. 8</reference>. God had said again and again, by his law and by his prophets, "<hi type="italic">Obey my voice,</hi> do as you are bidden, and all shall be well;" <hi type="italic">yet they obeyed not;</hi> and, because they were resolved not to submit their souls to God's commandments, they would not so much as incline their ears to them, but got as far as they could out of call: <hi type="italic">They walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart,</hi> followed their own inventions; every man did as his fancy and humour led him, right or wrong, lawful or unlawful, both in their devotions and in their conversations; see <reference osisRef="Jer.7.24">ch. vii. 24</reference>. What then could they expect, but to fall under the curse of the covenant, since they would not comply with the commands and conditions of it? <hi type="italic">Therefore I will bring upon them all the words of this covenant,</hi> that is, all the threatenings contained in it, because <hi type="italic">they did not what they were commanded.</hi> Note, The words of the covenant shall not fall to the ground. If we do not by our obedience qualify ourselves for the blessings of it, we shall by our disobedience bring ourselves under the curses of it. That which aggravated their defection from God, and rebellion against him, was that it was general, and as it were <hi type="italic">by consent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.9-Jer.11.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Jeremiah himself saw that many lived in open disobedience to God, but the Lord told him that the matter was worse than he thought of: <hi type="italic">A conspiracy is found among them,</hi> by him whose eye is upon the hidden works of darkness. There is a combination against God and religion, a dangerous design formed to overthrow God's government and bring in the pretenders, the counterfeit deities. This intimates that they were wilful and deliberate in wickedness (they rebelled against God, not through incogitancy, but presumptuously, and with a high hand),—that they were subtle and ingenious in wickedness, and carried on their plot against religion with a great deal of art and contrivance,—that they were linked together in the design, and, as is usual among conspirators, engaged to stand by one another in it and to live and die together; they were resolved to go through with it. A cursed conspiracy! O that there were not the like in our day! Observe, 1. What the conspiracy was. They designed to overthrow divine revelation, and set that aside, and persuade people not to hear, not to heed, the words of God. They did all they could to derogate from the authority of the scriptures and to lessen the value of them; they designed to draw people <hi type="italic">after other gods to serve them,</hi> to consult them as their oracles and make court to them as their benefactors. Human reason shall be their god, a light within their god, an infallible judge their god, saints and angels their gods, the god of this or the other nation shall be theirs; thus, under several disguises, they are in the same confederacy <hi type="italic">against the Lord and against his anointed.</hi> 2. Who were in conspiracy. One would have expected find some foreigners ring-leaders in it; but no, (1.) <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Jerusalem</hi> are in conspiracy with <hi type="italic">the men of Judah;</hi> city and country agree in this, however they may differ in other things. (2.) Those of this generation seem to be in conspiracy with those of the foregoing generation, to carry on the war from age to age against religion: <hi type="italic">They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers,</hi> and have risen up in their stead, <hi type="italic">a seed of evil-doers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">increase of sinful men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.32.14">Num. xxxii. 14</reference>. In Josiah's time there had been a reformation, but after this death the people returned to the idolatries which then they had renounced. (3.) Judah and Israel, the kingdom of the ten tribes and that of the two, that were often at daggers—drawing one with another, were yet <hi type="italic">in a conspiracy to break the covenant God had made with their fathers,</hi> even with the heads of all the twelve tribes. The house of Israel began the revolt, but the house of Judah soon came into the conspiracy. Now what else could be expected but that god should take severe methods, both for the chastising of the conspirators and the crushing of this conspiracy; for none ever hardened his heart thus against God and prospered? He that rolls this stone will find it return upon him.
entries.73bd8adae9553d1db810d8f8b0ad55bf5a7ccc1b: <div eID="gen17429" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Deplorable Condition of Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17430" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will bring evil upon them, which they shall not be able to escape; and though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then shall the cities of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem go, and cry unto the gods unto whom they offer incense: but they shall not save them at all in the time of their trouble. <hi type="super">13</hi> For <hi type="italic">according to</hi> the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah; and <hi type="italic">according to</hi> the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to <hi type="italic">that</hi> shameful thing, <hi type="italic">even</hi> altars to burn incense unto Baal. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up a cry or prayer for them: for I will not hear <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the time that they cry unto me for their trouble. <hi type="super">15</hi> What hath my beloved to do in mine house, <hi type="italic">seeing</hi> she hath wrought lewdness with many, and the holy flesh is passed from thee? when thou doest evil, then thou rejoicest. <hi type="super">16</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken. <hi type="super">17</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, that planted thee, hath pronounced evil against thee, for the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have done against themselves to provoke me to anger in offering incense unto Baal. <div eID="gen17430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17431" type="x-p"/> This paragraph, which contains so much of God's wrath, might very well be expected to follow upon that which goes next before, which contained so much of his people's sin. When God found so much evil among them we cannot think it strange if it follows, <hi type="italic">Therefore I will bring evil upon them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.11">v. 11</reference>), the evil of punishment for the evil of sin; and there is no remedy, no relief: the decree has gone forth and the sentence will be executed. <div eID="gen17431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17432" type="x-p"/> I. They cannot help themselves, but will be found too weak to contest with God's judgments: it is <hi type="italic">evil which they shall not be able to escape,</hi> or to <hi type="italic">go forth out of,</hi> by any evasion whatsoever. Note, Those that will not submit to God's government shall not be able to escape his wrath. There is no fleeing from his justice, no avoiding his cognizance. Evil pursues sinners and entangles them in snares out of which they cannot extricate themselves. <div eID="gen17432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17433" type="x-p"/> II. Their God will not help them; his providence shall no way favour them: <hi type="italic">Though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken to them.</hi> In their affliction they will seek the God whom before they slighted, and cry to him whom before they would not vouchsafe to speak to. But how can they expect to speed? For he has plainly told us that he that <hi type="italic">turns away his ears from hearing the law,</hi> as they did, for they <hi type="italic">inclined not their ear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.8">v. 8</reference>), even his prayer shall be an abomination to him, as the word of the Lord was now to them a reproach. <div eID="gen17433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17434" type="x-p"/> III. Their idols shall not help them, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">v. 12</reference>. They shall <hi type="italic">go, and cry to the gods to whom they</hi> now <hi type="italic">offer incense,</hi> and put them in mind of the costly services wherewith they had honoured them, expecting they should now have relief from them, but in vain. They shall be sent to the <hi type="italic">gods whom they served</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.37-Deut.32.38">Deut. xxxii. 37, 38</reference>), and what the better? <hi type="italic">They shall not save them at all,</hi> shall do nothing towards their salvation, nor give them any prospect of it; they shall not afford them the least comfort, nor relief, nor mitigation of their trouble. It is God only that is a friend at need, <hi type="italic">a present</hi> powerful <hi type="italic">help in time of trouble.</hi> The idols cannot help themselves; how then should they help their worshippers? Those that make idols of the world and the flesh will in vain have recourse to them in a day of distress. If the idols could have done any real kindness to their worshippers, they would have done it for this people, who had renounced the true God to embrace them, had multiplied them <hi type="italic">according to the number of their cities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">v. 13</reference>), nay, in Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">according to the number of their streets.</hi> Suspecting both their sufficiency and their readiness to help them, they must have many, lest a few would not serve; they must have them dispersed in every corner, lest they should be out of the way when they had occasion for them. In <hi type="italic">Jerusalem,</hi> the city which God had chosen to put his name there, publicly in the streets of Jerusalem, in every street, they had <hi type="italic">altars to that shameful thing,</hi> that <hi type="italic">shame,</hi> even to Baal, which they ought to have been ashamed of, with which they did reproach the Lord and bring confusion upon themselves. But now in their distress their many gods, and many altars, should stand them in stead. Note, Those that will not be ashamed of their commission of sin as a wicked thing will be ashamed of their expectations from sin as a fruitless thing. <div eID="gen17434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17435" type="x-p"/> IV. Jeremiah's prayers shall not help them, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">v. 14</reference>. What God had said to him before (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">ch. vii. 16</reference>) he here says again, <hi type="italic">Pray not thou for this people.</hi> This is not designed for a command to the prophet, so much as for a threatening to the people, that they should have no benefit by the prayers of their friends for them. God would give no encouragement to the prophets to pray for them, would not stir up the spirit of prayer, but cast a damp upon it, would put it into their hearts to pray, not for the body of the people, but for the remnant among them, to pray for their eternal salvation, not for their deliverance from the temporal judgments that were coming upon them; and what other prayers were put up for them should not be heard. Those are in a sad case indeed that are cut off from the benefit of prayer. "<hi type="italic">I will not hear them when they cry,</hi> and therefore to not thou pray for them." Note, Those that have so far thrown themselves out of God's favour that he will not hear their prayers cannot expect benefit by the prayers of others for them. <div eID="gen17435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17436" type="x-p"/> V. The profession they make of religion shall stand them in no stead, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">v. 15</reference>. They were originally God's <hi type="italic">beloved,</hi> his spouse, he was married to them by the covenant of peculiarity; even the unbelieving Jews are said to be <hi type="italic">beloved for the fathers' sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>. As such they had a place <hi type="italic">in God's house;</hi> they were admitted to worship in the courts of his temple; they partook of God's altar; they ate of the flesh of their peace-offerings here called the <hi type="italic">holy flesh,</hi> which God had the honour of and they had the comfort of. This they gloried in, and trusted to. What harm could come to those who were God's beloved, who were under the protection of his house? Even when they <hi type="italic">did evil</hi> yet <hi type="italic">they rejoiced</hi> and gloried in this, made a mighty noise of this. And <hi type="italic">when their evil was</hi> (so the margin reads it), when trouble came upon them, <hi type="italic">they rejoiced in this,</hi> and made this their confidence; but their confidence would deceive them, for God has rejected it, they themselves having forfeited the privileges they so much boasted of. They have <hi type="italic">wrought lewdness with many,</hi> have been guilty of spiritual whoredom, have worshipped many idols; and therefore, 1. God's temple will <hi type="italic">yield them no protection;</hi> it is fit that the adulteress, especially when she has so often repeated her whoredoms and has grown so impudent in them and irreclaimable, should be <hi type="italic">put away,</hi> and turned out of doors: "<hi type="italic">What has my beloved to do in my house?</hi> She is a scandal to it, and therefore it shall no longer be a shelter to her." 2. God's altar will yield them no satisfaction, nor can they expect any comfort from that: "<hi type="italic">The holy flesh has passed from thee,</hi> that is, an end will soon be put to thy sacrifices, when the temple shall be laid in ruins; and where then will the holy flesh be, that thou art so proud of?" A holy heart will be a comfort to us when the holy flesh has passed from us; an inward principle of grace will make up the want of the outward means of grace. But woe unto us if the departure of the holy flesh be accompanied with the departure of the Holy Spirit. <div eID="gen17436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17437" type="x-p"/> VI. God's former favours to them shall stand them in no stead, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.16-Jer.11.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Their remembrance of them shall be no comfort to them under their troubles, and God's remembrance of them shall be no argument for their relief. 1. It is true God had done great things for them; that people had been favourites above any people under the sun; they had been the darlings of heaven. God had <hi type="italic">called Israel's name a green olive-tree,</hi> and had made them so, for he miscalls nothing; he had <hi type="italic">planted</hi> them (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.17">v. 17</reference>), had formed them into a people, with all the advantages they could have to make them a fruitful and flourishing people, so good was their law and so good was their land. One would think no other than that a people so planted, so watered, so cultivated, should be, as the olive-tree is, ever green, in respect both of piety and prosperity, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Ps. lii. 8</reference>. God called them <hi type="italic">fair and of goodly fruit,</hi> both good for food and pleasant to the eye, both amiable and serviceable to God and man, for which the greenness and fatness of the olive both are honoured, <reference osisRef="Judg.9.9">Judg. ix. 9</reference>. 2. It is as true that they have done evil things against God. He had planted them a green olive, a good olive, but they had degenerated into a <hi type="italic">wild olive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom. xi. 17</reference>. Both <hi type="italic">the house of Israel</hi> and the <hi type="italic">house of Judah</hi> had <hi type="italic">done evil,</hi> had <hi type="italic">provoked God to anger in burning incense unto Baal,</hi> setting up other mediators between them and the supreme God besides the promised Messiah; nay, setting up other gods in competition with the true and living God, for they had <hi type="italic">gods many,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">lords many.</hi> 3. When they have conducted themselves so ill they can expect no other than that, notwithstanding what good he has done to them and designed for them, he should now bring upon them the evil he has <hi type="italic">pronounced against them.</hi> He that planted this green olive-tree, and expected fruit from it, finding it barren and grown wild, <hi type="italic">has kindled fire upon it,</hi> to burn it as it stands; for, being without fruit, it is <hi type="italic">twice dead, plucked up by the roots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.12">Jude 12</reference>), it is <hi type="italic">cut down and cast into the fire,</hi> the fittest place for trees that cumber the ground, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.10">Matt. iii. 10</reference>. The <hi type="italic">branches of it,</hi> the <hi type="italic">high and lofty boughs</hi> (so the word signifies), are <hi type="italic">broken</hi> are <hi type="italic">broken down,</hi> both princes and priests cut off. And thus it proves that the evil done against God, to <hi type="italic">provoke him to anger,</hi> is really done <hi type="italic">against themselves;</hi> they <hi type="italic">wrong their own souls;</hi> God is out of their reach, but they ruin themselves. See <reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">ch. vii. 19</reference>. Note, Every sin against God is a sin against ourselves, and so it will be found sooner or later.
entries.0dbd37fcf0c28e7332b3b7cd9e534b18c4b1ee1c: <div eID="gen17437" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conspiracy against Jeremiah; Destruction of the Men of Anathoth. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath given me knowledge <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> and I know <hi type="italic">it:</hi> then thou showedst me their doings. <hi type="super">19</hi> But I <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a lamb <hi type="italic">or</hi> an ox <hi type="italic">that</hi> is brought to the slaughter; and I knew not that they had devised devices against me, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered. <hi type="super">20</hi> But, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> of hosts, that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart, let me see thy vengeance on them: for unto thee have I revealed my cause. <hi type="super">21</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that thou die not by our hand: <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, Behold, I will punish them: the young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine: <hi type="super">23</hi> And there shall be no remnant of them: for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the year of their visitation. <div eID="gen17438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17439" type="x-p"/> The prophet Jeremiah has much in his writings concerning himself, much more than Isaiah had, the times he lived in being very troublesome. Here we have (as it should seem) the beginning of his sorrows, which arose from the people of his own city, Anathoth, a priest's city, and yet a malignant one. Observe here, <div eID="gen17439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17440" type="x-p"/> I. Their plot against him, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">v. 19</reference>. They <hi type="italic">devised devices against him,</hi> laid their heads together to contrive how they might be in the most plausible and effectual manner the death of him. Malice is ingenious in its devices, as well as industrious in its prosecutions. They said concerning Jeremiah, <hi type="italic">Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof</hi>—a proverbial expression, meaning, "Let us utterly destroy him root and branch. Let us destroy both the father and the family" (as, when Naboth was put to death for treason, his sons were put to death with him), or rather "both the prophet and the prophecy; let us kill the one and defeat the other. <hi type="italic">Let us cut him off from the land of the living,</hi> as a false prophet, and load him with ignominy and disgrace, <hi type="italic">that his name may be no more remembered</hi> with respect. Let us sink his reputation, and so spoil the credit of his predictions." This was their plot; and 1. It was a cruel one; but so cruel have the persecutors of God's prophets been. They <hi type="italic">hunt for</hi> no less than <hi type="italic">the precious life,</hi> and very precious the lives are that they hunt for. But, (2.) It was a baffled one. They thought to put an end to his days, but he survived most of his enemies; they thought to blast his memory, but it lives to this day, and will be blessed while time lasts. <div eID="gen17440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17441" type="x-p"/> II. The information which God gave him of this conspiracy against him. He knew nothing of it himself, so artfully had they concealed it; he came to Anathoth, meaning no harm to them and therefore fearing no harm from them, <hi type="italic">like a lamb or an ox,</hi> that thinks he is driven as usual to the field, <hi type="italic">when he is brought to the slaughter;</hi> so little did poor Jeremiah dream of the design his citizens that hated him had upon him. None of his friends could, and none of his enemies would, give him any notice of his danger, that he might shift for his own safety, as Paul's sister's son gave him intelligence of the Jews that were lying in wait for him. There is but a step between Jeremiah and death; but then <hi type="italic">the Lord gave him knowledge of it,</hi> by dream or vision, or impression upon his spirit, that he might save himself, as the king of Israel did upon the notice Elisha gave him, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.10">2 Kings vi. 10</reference>. Thus he came to <hi type="italic">know it.</hi> God <hi type="italic">showed him their doings;</hi> and such were their devices that the discovering of them was the defeating of them. If God had not let him know his own danger, it would have been improved by unreasonable men against the reputation of his predictions, that he who foretold the ruin of his country could not foresee his own peril and avoid it. See what care God takes of his prophets: He <hi type="italic">suffers no man to do them wrong;</hi> all the rage of their enemies cannot prevail to take them off till they have finished their testimony. God knows all the secret designs of his and his people's enemies, and can, when he pleases, make them know. <hi type="italic">A bird of the air shall carry the voice.</hi> <div eID="gen17441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17442" type="x-p"/> III. His appeal to God hereupon, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.20">v. 20</reference>. His eye is to God as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts, that judges righteously.</hi> It is a matter of comfort to us, when men deal unjustly with us, that we have a God to go to who does and will plead the cause of injured innocency and appear against the injurious. God's justice, which is a terror to the wicked, is a comfort to the godly. His eye is towards him as the God that <hi type="italic">tries the reins and the heart,</hi> that perfectly sees what is in man, what are his thoughts and intents. He knew the integrity that was in Jeremiah's heart, and that he was not the man they represented him to be. He knew the wickedness that was in their hearts, though ever so cunningly concealed and disguised. Now, 1. Jeremiah prays judgment against them: "<hi type="italic">Let me see thy vengeance on them,</hi> that is, do justice between me and them in such a way as thou pleasest." Some think there was something of human frailty in this prayer; at least Christ has taught us another lesson, both by precept and by pattern, which is to pray for our persecutors. Others think it comes from a pure zeal for the glory of God and a pious and prophetic indignation against men that were by profession priests, the Lord's ministers, and yet were so desperately wicked as to fly out against one that did them no harm, merely for the service he did to God. This petition was a prediction that he should see God's vengeance on them. 2. He refers his cause entirely to the judgment of God: "<hi type="italic">Unto thee have I revealed my cause;</hi> to thee I have committed it, not desiring nor expecting to interest any other in it." Note, It is our comfort, when we are wronged, that we have a God to commit our cause to, and our duty to commit it to him, with a resolution to acquiesce in his definitive sentence, to subscribe, and not prescribe, to him. <div eID="gen17442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17443" type="x-p"/> IV. Judgment given against his persecutors, <hi type="italic">the men of Anathoth.</hi> It was to no purpose for him to appeal to the courts at Jerusalem, he could not have justice done him there: the priests there would stand by the priests at Anathoth, and rather second them than discountenance them; but God will <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> take cognizance of the cause himself, and we are sure that <hi type="italic">his judgment is according to truth.</hi> Here is, 1. Their crime recited, on which the sentence is grounded, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">v. 21</reference>. They sought the prophet's life, for they forbad him to prophesy upon pain of death; they were resolved either to silence him or to slay him. The provocation he gave them was his prophesying <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord</hi> without license from those that were the governors of the city which he was a member of, and not prophesying such smooth things as they always bespoke. Their forbidding him to prophesy was in effect seeking his life, for it was seeking to defeat the end and business of his life and to rob him of the comfort of it. It is as bad to God's faithful ministers to have their mouth stopped as to have their breath stopped. But especially when it was resolved that if he did prophesy, as certainly he would notwithstanding their inhibition, he should <hi type="italic">die by their hand;</hi> they would be accusers, judges, executioners, and all. It used to be said that <hi type="italic">a prophet could not perish but at Jerusalem,</hi> for there the great council sat; but so bitter were the men of Anathoth against Jeremiah that they would undertake to be the death of him themselves. A prophet then shall find not only no honour, but no favour, in his own country. 2. The sentence passed upon them for this crime, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.22-Jer.11.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. God says, <hi type="italic">I will punish them;</hi> let me alone to deal with them. <hi type="italic">I will visit</hi> this <hi type="italic">upon them;</hi> so the word is. God will enquire into it and reckon for it. Two of God's four sore judgments shall serve to ruin their town:—<hi type="italic">The sword</hi> shall devour their <hi type="italic">young men,</hi> though they were young priests, not men of war (their character shall not be their protection), and <hi type="italic">famine</hi> shall destroy the children, <hi type="italic">sons and daughters,</hi> that tarry at home, which is a more grievous death than that by the sword, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.9">Lam. iv. 9</reference>. The destruction shall be final (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">There shall be no remnant of them left,</hi> none to be the seed of another generation. They sought Jeremiah's life, and therefore they shall die; they would destroy him <hi type="italic">root and branch,</hi> that <hi type="italic">his name</hi> might be <hi type="italic">no more remembered,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">there shall be no remnant of them;</hi> and herein the Lord is righteous. Thus <hi type="italic">evil is brought upon them, even the year of their visitation,</hi> and that is evil enough, a recompence according to their deserts. Then shall Jeremiah <hi type="italic">see his desire upon his enemies.</hi> Note, Their condition is sad who have the prayers of good ministers and good people against them.  <chapter eID="Jer.11"/> <div eID="gen17443" type="x-p"/>

Judah's Revolt from It, and God's Consequent Wrath.</title> <div sID="gen17447" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9844"/><hi type="bold">2. this covenant--</hi>alluding to the book of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.26">De 31:26</reference>) found in the temple by Hilkiah the high priest, five years after Jeremiah's call to the prophetic office (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.8-2Kgs.23.25">2Ki 22:8-23:25</reference>).<div eID="gen17447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hear ye--</hi>Others besides Jeremiah were to promulgate God's will to the people; it was the duty of the priests to read the law to them (Mal 2:7). <div eID="gen17448" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">De 27:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Ga 3:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17449" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d049bbb567e5443a4cf7767392c8f5f22c9d0c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9846"/><div sID="gen17450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9846"/><hi type="bold">4. in the day--</hi>that is, when. The Sinaitic covenant was made some time after the exodus, but the two events are so connected as to be viewed as one.<div eID="gen17450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iron furnace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">De 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.51">1Ki 8:51</reference>). "Furnace" expresses the searching ordeal; "iron," the long duration of it. The furnace was of earth, not of iron (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>); a furnace, in heat and duration enough to melt even iron. God's deliverance of them from such an ordeal aggravates their present guilt.<div eID="gen17451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do them--</hi>namely, the words of the covenant (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">Jr 11:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17453" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.26.3">Le 26:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen17453" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e1496705f1ba86b57cc35ce870847a7ceca6143: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9847"/><div sID="gen17454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9847"/><hi type="bold">5. oath--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.105.9">Psa 105:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen17454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a land flowing with milk and honey--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Num.14.8">Nu 14:8</reference>).<div eID="gen17455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is this day--</hi>These are the concluding words of God to the Israelites when formerly brought out of Egypt, "Obey ... that I may at this time make good the promise I made to your fathers, to give," &c. [Maurer]. English Version makes the words apply to Jeremiah's time, "As ye know at this time, that God's promise has been fulfilled," namely, in Israel's acquisition of Canaan.<div eID="gen17456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17457" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">So be it--</hi>Hebrew, Amen. Taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.27.15-Deut.27.26">De 27:15-26</reference>. Jeremiah hereby solemnly concurs in the justice of the curses pronounced there (see <reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">Jr 11:3</reference>). <div eID="gen17457" type="x-p"/>

Jeremiah was to take a prophetic tour throughout Judah, to proclaim everywhere the denunciations in the book of the law found in the temple.<div eID="gen17458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hear ... do--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.2.13">Ro 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.22">Jas 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen17459" type="x-p"/>

entries.ebb92b6af547e4f0e24c79b0e8b4db5184234dd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9850"/><div sID="gen17461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9850"/><hi type="bold">8. imagination--</hi>rather, "stubbornness."<div eID="gen17461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will bring--</hi>The words, "even unto this day" (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">Jr 11:7</reference>), confirm English Version rather than the rendering of Rosenmuller: "I brought upon them."<div eID="gen17462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17463" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">words--</hi>threats (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">Jr 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.15-Deut.27.26">De 27:15-26</reference>). <div eID="gen17463" type="x-p"/>
entries.0eb1b3dbb913a2659efb5af23cb4833167c78785: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9851"/><div sID="gen17464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9851"/><hi type="bold">9. conspiracy--</hi>a deliberate combination against God and against Josiah's reformation. Their idolatry is not the result of a hasty impulse (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.5">Psa 83:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.25">Eze 22:25</reference>). <div eID="gen17464" type="x-p"/>
entries.a38715211f8f1fe0a3d344b9724c7b19029f51df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9852"/><div sID="gen17465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9852"/><hi type="bold">11. cry unto me--</hi>contrasted with "cry unto the gods," (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">Jr 11:12</reference>).<div eID="gen17465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17466" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not hearken--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.18.41">Psa 18:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Pr 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.4">Mi 3:4</reference>). <div eID="gen17466" type="x-p"/>
entries.826f9a6b3882d8e340bc161f07e234ead6f57d8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9853"/><div sID="gen17467" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9853"/><hi type="bold">12. cry unto the gods ... not save--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.37">De 32:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.38">38</reference>). Compare this verse and beginning of <reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jr 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.28">Jr 2:28</reference>.<div eID="gen17467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the time of their trouble--</hi>that is, calamity (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>). <div eID="gen17468" type="x-p"/>
entries.b468d9f419c87d54ab78aa250349ca89fe96de6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9854"/><div sID="gen17469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9854"/><hi type="bold">13. shameful thing--</hi>Hebrew, "shame," namely, the idol, not merely shameful, but the essence of all that is shameful (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.24">Jr 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">Ho 9:10</reference>), which will bring shame and confusion on yourselves [Calvin]. <div eID="gen17469" type="x-p"/>
entries.66d8ef821bf93f69264163a6770fca4b66c4ce43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9855"/><div sID="gen17470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9855"/>14. There is a climax of guilt which admits of no further intercessory prayer (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Ex 32:10</reference>, in the Chaldee version, "leave off praying"; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.1">1Sa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.35">15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1Jo 5:16</reference>). Our mind should be at one with God in all that He is doing, even in the rejection of the reprobate.<div eID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17471" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for their trouble--</hi>on account of their trouble. Other manuscripts read, "in the time of their trouble;" a gloss from <reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">Jr 11:12</reference>. <div eID="gen17471" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4a9e869b419824eb216cf0adc4399b3ef170859: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9856"/><div sID="gen17472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9856"/><hi type="bold">15. my beloved--</hi>My elect people, Judea; this aggravates their ingratitude (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jr 12:7</reference>).<div eID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lewdness with many--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.25">Eze 16:25</reference>). Rather, "that great (or, manifold) enormity"; literally, "the enormity, the manifold"; namely, their idolatry, which made their worship of God in the temple a mockery (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.7.10">Jr 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.39">Eze 23:39</reference>) [Henderson].<div eID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hag.2.12-Hag.2.14">Hag 2:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>), namely, the sacrifices, which, through the guilt of the Jews, were no longer holy, that is, acceptable to God. The sacrifices on which they relied will, therefore, no longer protect them. Judah is represented as a priest's wife, who, by adultery, has forfeited her share in the flesh of the sacrifices, and yet boasts of her prerogative at the very same time [Horsley].<div eID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17475" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when thou doest evil--</hi>literally, "when thy evil" (is at hand). Piscator translates, "When thy calamity is at hand (according to God's threats), thou gloriest" (against God, instead of humbling thyself). English Version is best (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.2.14">Pr 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen17475" type="x-p"/>
entries.b88a13ae84dffe5ee6860da025dff996017021df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9857"/><div sID="gen17476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9857"/><hi type="bold">16. called thy name--</hi>made thee.<div eID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">olive--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Psa 52:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Ro 11:17</reference>). The "olive" is chosen to represent the adoption of Judah by the free grace of God, as its oil is the image of richness (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">104:15</reference>).<div eID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... noise of ... tumult--</hi>or, "at the noise," &c., namely, at the tumult of the invading army (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">Is 13:4</reference>) [Maurer]. Or, rather, "with the sound of a mighty voice," namely, that of God, that is, the thunder; thus there is no confusion of metaphors. The tree stricken with lightning has "fire kindled upon it, and the branches are broken," at one and the same time [Houbigant]. <div eID="gen17478" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec4d9e093eacd18e51b585a3a42060a1045a1818: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9858"/><div sID="gen17479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9858"/><hi type="bold">17. that planted thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.21">Jr 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Is 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17480" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against themselves--</hi>The sinner's sin is to his own hurt (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.7.19">Jr 7:19</reference>). <div eID="gen17480" type="x-p"/>
entries.23b015b4d3c329f1030bd924a5f4ad8d56ff5243: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9859"/><div sID="gen17481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9859"/>18-19. Jeremiah here digresses to notice the attempt on his life plotted by his townsmen of Anathoth. He had no suspicion of it, until Jehovah revealed it to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jr 12:6</reference>).<div eID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord ... thou--</hi>The change of person from the third to the second accords with the excited feelings of the prophet.<div eID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>when I was in peril of my life.<div eID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their doings--</hi>those of the men of Anathoth. His thus alluding to them, before he has mentioned their name, is due to his excitement. <div eID="gen17484" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd75f0da313fc0e06bd3134912469da8f4fe1ecd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9861"/><div sID="gen17488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9861"/><hi type="bold">20. triest ... heart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.2.23">Re 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revealed--</hi>committed my cause. Jeremiah's wish for vengeance was not personal but ministerial, and accorded with God's purpose revealed to him against the enemies alike of God and of His servant (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.34">Psa 37:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.54.7">54:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.8">112:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">118:7</reference>). <div eID="gen17489" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6e43450a042727bd55cf0a4c2fd4b4f800ed59f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9862"/><div sID="gen17490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9862"/><hi type="bold">21. Prophesy not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Is 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.12">Am 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.6">Mi 2:6</reference>). If Jeremiah had not uttered his denunciatory predictions, they would not have plotted against him. None were more bitter than his own fellow townsmen. Compare the conduct of the Nazarites towards Jesus of Nazareth (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.24-Luke.4.29">Lu 4:24-29</reference>). <div eID="gen17490" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b6c99ea61f30e8934e2f99804b29709010edb24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9863"/><div sID="gen17491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9863"/>22. The retribution of their intended murder shall be in kind; just as in Messiah's case (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.8-Ps.69.28">Psa 69:8-28</reference>). <div eID="gen17491" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2c8bc4feb600cc4adada8b2ff1de2868be210ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9864"/><div sID="gen17492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9864"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.12">Jr 23:12</reference>).<div eID="gen17492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17493" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the year of ... visitation--</hi>The Septuagint translates, "in the year of their," &c., that is, at the time when I shall visit them in wrath. Jerome supports English Version. "Year" often means a determined time. <chapter eID="Jer.11"/>

entries.4887d3f990e52462dec8563e0de3d69203b7fad0: <div eID="gen29538" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29539" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29540" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29540" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29539" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29541" type="x-p"/> The prophet proclaims the tenor of God's covenant with the Jews of old, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.1-Jer.11.5">Jer 11:1-5</reference>; and then reproves them for their hereditary disobedience, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.6-Jer.11.19">Jer 11:6-19</reference>. In consequence of this the Almighty is introduced, declaring he will show them no pity, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.11-Jer.11.13">Jer 11:11-13</reference>; forbidding Jeremiah to intercede, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">Jer 11:14</reference>; rejecting their sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jer 11:15</reference>; and in a word, condemning this fair but unfruitful tree to the fire, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.16">Jer 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.17">Jer 11:17</reference>. In what remains of the chapter the prophet predicts evil to his neighbors of Anathoth, who had conspired against him, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.18-Jer.11.23">Jer 11:18-23</reference>. "Let us," said they, "destroy this tree, with the fruit thereof," etc., alluding to what Jeremiah had said in the sixteenth verse. <div eID="gen29541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29542" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29543" type="x-p"/> The word that came to Jeremiah - This discourse is supposed to have been delivered in the first year of the reign of Zedekiah. See Dahler.
entries.38712f68cf1aed5354beafa10bb74dcb583180bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29544" type="x-p"/> Hear ye the words of this covenant - It is possible that the prophet caused the words of the covenant made with their fathers in the desert (<reference osisRef="Exo.24.4-Exo.24.8">Exo 24:4-8</reference>) to be read to them on this occasion; or, at least, the blessings and the cursings which Moses caused to be pronounced to the people as soon as they had set foot in Canaan, Deuteronomy 27, 28.
entries.e8ef21d7d7b630bbaa397604608b9d28097fc9c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29545" type="x-p"/> Cursed be the man that obeyeth not - After the reading, the prophet appears to sum up the things contained in what was read to them; as if he had said, "Ye hear what the Lord saith unto you: remember, the sum of it is this: The man is cursed who obeyeth not; and he is blessed who obeys. From these declarations God will not depart."
entries.f9ecf2a12e504aeff4ee6c14cdb0f154596101ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29546" type="x-p"/> So be it, O Lord - Let thy promises be fulfilled; and let the incorrigible beware of thy threatenings!
entries.785e9ba2cfc36d92ea60a8f7ee656d7ce52e7fa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29547" type="x-p"/> Proclaim all these words - Let the same covenant, with the blessings and cursings, be read in every city of Judah, and in all the streets of Jerusalem, that all the people may know their duty, their privileges, and their danger.
entries.01f0baba97a30a8d74dcd0180f65bf0cd7575063: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29548" type="x-p"/> A conspiracy is found - They were all fratres conjurati, sworn brothers, determined to cast off the Divine yoke, and no longer to have God to reign over them.
entries.0d20fd13146cb7fa41ce797099b6a784dcb0f540: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29549" type="x-p"/> They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers - A great reformation had taken place under the reign of Josiah, and the public worship of idols had been abolished, and most of the high places destroyed; but under the reign of his son and his successors, they had turned back again to idolatry, and were become worse than ever. It required a captivity to cure them of this propensity: and God sent one: after that, there was no idolatry among the Jews.
entries.32f1c8f193c687a9b03c3cf6d77998e77192f449: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29550" type="x-p"/> Go, and cry unto the gods - See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.28">Jer 2:28</reference>.
entries.3fee29db054f3d34b78396dfe1a42f89cdac00ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29551" type="x-p"/> Therefore pray not thou for this people - I am determined to give them up into the hands of their enemies; I will neither hear thy intercession, nor regard their prayers. Their measure is full.
entries.db870fe07c0b82416c1202c08e91972ba2e80a90: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29552" type="x-p"/> What hath my beloved to do in mine house - This has been supposed to refer to Abraham, Moses, or such eminent servants of God, whose intercession was very powerful. Were even they to appear as intercessors, their prayer should not be regarded. Others think that this is an endearing expression which properly belonged to the Israelites. When God took them into covenant with himself, they were espoused to him, and therefore his beloved; but now that they have forsaken him, and joined themselves to another, what have they to do with his house or its ordinances, which they wish now to frequent with vows and sacrifices, when they see the evil fast coming upon them? This is probably the sense of this very obscure passage. Dr. Blayney translates, "What hath my beloved to do in my house whilst she practiseth wickedness? Shall vows and holy flesh (sacrifices) be allowed to come from thee? When thou art malignant, shalt thou rejoice?"
entries.d3632f9733d896bafbf7f51b4baad4d14c3c4c95: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29553" type="x-p"/> The Lord called thy name, A green olive tree - That is, he made thee like a green olive - fair, flourishing, and fruitful; but thou art degenerated, and God hath given the Chaldeans permission to burn thee up.
entries.4da35b151ababc82bdaad5012b8c3327d69f8509: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29554" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath given me knowledge of it - The men of Anathoth had conspired against his life, because he reproved them for their sins, and denounced the judgments of God against them. Of this God had given him a secret warning, that he might be on his guard.
entries.8f0d6b78f639d94172df2cb61762c77bc39c79df: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29555" type="x-p"/> I was like a lamb or an ox - Dahler translates, "I was like a fattened lamb that is led to the slaughter." Blayney, "I was like a tame lamb that is led to slaughter." The word אלוף alluph, which we translate ox, is taken by both as an adjective, qualifying the noun כבש kebes, a lamb. It may probably signify a lamb brought up in the house-fed at home, (אלוף alluph), instructed or nourished at home; perfectly innocent and unsuspecting, while leading to the slaughter. This meaning the word will bear in Arabic, for alaf signifies accustomed, familiar, (to or with any person or thing); a companion, a comrade, an intimate friend. I therefore think that ככבש אלוף kechebes alluph signifies, like the familiar lamb - the lamb bred up in the house, in a state of friendship with the family. The people of Anathoth were Jeremiah's townsmen; he was born and bred among them; they were his familiar friends; and now they lay wait for his life! All the Versions understood אלוף alluph as an epithet of כבש kebes, a chosen, simple, innocent lamb. <div eID="gen29555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29556" type="x-p"/> Let us destroy the tree with the fruit - Let us slay the prophet, and his prophecies will come to an end. The Targum has, Let us put mortal poison in his food; and all the Versions understand it something in the same way.
entries.f38713aef96f4832bb28c174d2b79f4cf9119e1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29557" type="x-p"/> Let me see thy vengeance on them - Rather, I shall see (אראה ereh) thy punishment indicted on them.
entries.520beec462c70aa142f2819e0441ce1d46f0a240: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen29557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29558" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will punish them - And the punishment is, Their young men shall die by the sword of the Chaldeans; and their sons and daughters shall die by the famine that shall come on the land through the desolations occasioned by the Chaldean army.
entries.921c31faefb9e6eb481921e53b5d6f5b99b89457: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen29558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29559" type="x-p"/> The year of their visitation - This punishment shall come in that year in which I shall visit their iniquities upon them.  <chapter eID="Jer.11"/> <div eID="gen29559" type="x-p"/>

entries.9f5645ecfde4353c5613258367088aa0a5b19906: <reference osisRef="Jer.11.1-Jer.11.8">Jer 11:1-8</reference> <hi type="italic">"The word which came to Jeremiah from Jahveh, saying:</hi> Jer 11:2. <hi type="italic">Hear ye the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem,</hi> Jer 11:3. <hi type="italic">And say thou to them: Thus hath Jahve, the God of Israel, said: Cursed is the man that heareth not the words of this covenant,</hi> Jer 11:4. <hi type="italic">Which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, saying: Hearken to my voice, and do them according to all which I command you; so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God;</hi> Jer 11:5. <hi type="italic">That I may perform the oath which I have sworn unto your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. And I answered and said: So be it, Jahveh.</hi> Jer 11:6. <hi type="italic">Then said Jahveh to me: Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying: Hear ye the words of this covenant and do them.</hi> Jer 11:7. <hi type="italic">For I have testified to your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt unto this day, testifying from early morning on: Hearken to my voice!</hi> Jer 11:8. <hi type="italic">But they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear, but walked each in the stubbornness of their evil heart; and so I brought on them all the words of this covenant which I have commanded them to do, and they have not done them."</hi> <div eID="gen13958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> The form of address, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.2">Jer 11:2</reference> : hear ye (שׁמעוּ), and speak ye (דּבּרתּם), is noteworthy since we are not told who are to hear and speak; while at <reference osisRef="Jer.11.3">Jer 11:3</reference>, in ואמרתּ Jeremiah receives the commission to declare the words of the covenant to the people, and to make known in the cities of Judah, etc. (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.6">Jer 11:6</reference>). The difficulty is not removed by the plan adopted by Hitz. and Graf from the lxx, of changing ודבּרתּם into ודבּרתּם, "and speak them;" for the שׁמעוּ remains to be dealt with. To whom then, is it addressed? Schleussner proposed to change it into שׁמעה - a purely arbitrary change. In <reference osisRef="Jer.11.4">Jer 11:4</reference> "hearing" is used in the sense of giving ear to, obeying. And in no other sense can it be taken in Jer 11:1. "The words of this covenant" are, as is clear from the succeeding context, the words of the covenant recorded in the Pentateuch, known from the reading of the Torah. The call to hear the words thereof can only have the meaning of: to give ear to them, take them to heart. Hence Chr. B. Mich. and Schnur. have referred the words to the Jews: Listen, ye Jews and ye citizens of Jerusalem, to the words of the covenant, and make them know to one another, and exhort one another to observe them. But this paraphrase is hardly consistent with the wording of the verse. Others fancied that the priests and elders were addressed; but if so, these must necessarily have been named. Clearly it is to the prophets in general that the words are spoken, as Kimchi observed; and we must not take "hear ye" as if the covenant was unknown to the prophets, but as intended to remind the prophets of them, that they might enforce them upon the people. Taken thus, this introductory verse serves to exalt the importance of the truths mentioned, to mark them out as truths which God had commanded all the prophets to proclaim. If it be the prophets in general who are addressed in <reference osisRef="Jer.11.2">Jer 11:2</reference>, the transition to "and say thou" is easily explained. Jeremiah, too, must himself do that which was the bounden duty of all the prophets, must make the men of Judah and Jerusalem call to mind the curse overhanging transgressors of the covenant. The words: Cursed is the man, etc., are taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.27.26">Deu 27:26</reference>, from the directions for the engagement to keep the covenant, which the people were to solemnise upon their entry into Canaan, and which, acc. to Jos 8:30., they did solemnise. The quotation is made freely from memory. Instead of "that heareth not the words of this covenant," we find in Deut. <hi type="italic">l.c</hi>.: "the confirmeth not (יקים) the words of this law to do them." The choice there of the word יקים is suggested by its connection with the act of solemnisation enjoined. The recitation and promulgation of the law upon Mount Gerizim and Ebal (Deut 27) had no other aim than that of solemnly binding the people to keep or follow the law; and this is what Jeremiah means by "hearing." The law to be established is the law of the covenant, i.e., the covenant made by Jahveh with Israel, and spoken of in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deu 28:68</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.29.8">Deu 29:8</reference> as the "words of this covenant." This covenant, which Moses had made with the sons of Israel in the land of Moab (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deu 28:68</reference>), was but a renewal of that solemnly concluded at Sinai (Ex 24). And so Jeremiah speaks of this covenant as the one which Jahveh commanded the fathers in the day, i.e., at the time, of their leaving Egypt. "In the day that," etc., as in Jer 7:22. "Out of the iron furnace:" this metaphor for the affliction endured by Israel in Egypt is taken from Deu 4:20. The words: hearken unto my voice and do <hi type="italic">them</hi> (the words of the covenant), suggest <reference osisRef="Deut.27.1-Deut.27.2">Deu 27:1-2</reference>; and the words: so shall ye be my people, suggest <reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">Deu 29:12</reference>, a passage which itself points back to ex. <reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer 6:7</reference> (Jer 19:5.), <reference osisRef="Lev.27.12">Lev 27:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.6">Deu 7:6</reference>, etc. That I may establish, i.e., perform, the oath which I have sworn unto your fathers, i.e., the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.8">Deu 7:8</reference>, etc.), promising to give them a land flowing, etc. The frequently repeated description of the promised land; cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exo 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.17">Exo 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.6.3">Deu 6:3</reference>, etc. כּיּום , as in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.30">Deu 2:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">Deu 4:20</reference>, etc., is not: at this time, now (Graf), but: as this day, meaning: as is even now the case, sc. that ye still possess this precious land. The assenting reply of the prophet: אמן יהוה, yea, or so be it (γένοιτο, lxx), Lord, corresponds to the אמן with which the people, acc. to Deu 27:15., were to take on themselves the curses attached to the breaking of the law, curses which they did take on themselves when the law was promulgated in Canaan. As the whole congregation did on that occasion, so here the prophet, by his "yea," expresses his adherence to the covenant, and admits that the engagement is yet in full force for the congregation of God; and at the same time indicates that he, on his part, is ready to labour for the fulfilment of the covenant, so that the people may not become liable to the curse of the law.
entries.19df34608fb16244fa0eaa0caf59d894172174e9: <reference osisRef="Jer.11.9-Jer.11.13">Jer 11:9-13</reference> <hi type="italic">The people’s breach of the covenant, and the consequences of this. -</hi> Jer 11:9. <hi type="italic">"And Jahveh said unto me: Conspiracy is found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.</hi> Jer 11:10. <hi type="italic">They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to give ear to my words, and they are gone after other gods to serve them; the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers.</hi> Jer 11:11. <hi type="italic">Behold, I bring evil upon them, from which they cannot escape; and though they cry to me, I will not hear them.</hi> Jer 11:12. <hi type="italic">And the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem shall go and cry unto the gods unto whom they offer incense, but they shall not help them in the time of their trouble.</hi> Jer 11:13. <hi type="italic">For as many as are thy cities, so many are thy gods become, O Judah; and as many as are the streets of Jerusalem, so many altars have ye set up to Shame, altars to offer odours to Baal."</hi> <div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah is once more to enforce the words of the covenant upon the people, because they have broken the covenant, returned to the idolatry of the fathers. Conspiracy is found, is to be seen. The people’s defection from Jahveh, their breach of faith towards the covenant God, is called conspiracy, because it had become as universal as if it had been initiated by a formal preconcertment. "The former fathers," forefathers of the people, are the Israelites under Moses, who broke the covenant by idolatry while still at Sinai, and those of the time of the Judges. With והמּה the subject is changed; "they" are not the forefathers, but the prophet’s contemporaries. In the last clause of <reference osisRef="Jer.11.10">Jer 11:10</reference> is comprehended the apostasy of the whole people: Like Israel, Judah too has broken the covenant. Israel has been punished for this by being cast out among the heathen, the like doom awaits Judah.
entries.5bfff73f800f0f8033f276330c7b6c10d6c09852: <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14-Jer.11.17">Jer 11:14-17</reference> <hi type="italic">Neither entreaty on their behalf nor their hypocritical worship will avert judgment. - </hi> Jer 11:14. <hi type="italic">"But thou, pray not for this people, neither lift up for them cry or prayer; for I hear them not in the time that they cry unto me for their trouble.</hi> Jer 11:15. <hi type="italic">What would my beloved in my house? they who practise guile? Shall vows and holy flesh remove they calamity from thee? then mayest thou exult.</hi> Jer 11:16. <hi type="italic">A green olive, fair for its goodly fruit, Jahveh called thy name; with the noise of great tumult He set fire to it, and its branches brake.</hi> Jer 11:17. <hi type="italic">And Jahveh of hosts, that planted thee, hath decreed evil against thee, for the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah which they themselves have done, to provoke me, in that they have offered odours to Baal."</hi> <div eID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> We have already, in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jer 7:16</reference>, met with the declaration that the Lord will not accept any intercession for the covenant-breaking people (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">Jer 11:14</reference>); the termination of this verse differs slightly in the turn to takes. -  בּעד רעתם the ancient commentators have almost unanimously rendered: <hi type="italic">tempore mali eorum</hi>, as if they had read בּעת (this is, in fact, the reading of some codd.); but hardly on sufficient grounds. בּעד gives a suitable sense, with the force of the Greek ἀμφί, which, like the German <hi type="italic">um</hi>, passes into the sense of <hi type="italic">wegen</hi>, as the English <hi type="italic">about</hi> passes into that of <hi type="italic">concerning</hi>. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15-Jer.11.17">Jer 11:15-17</reference> we have the reason why the Lord will hear neither the prophet’s supplication nor the people’s cry in their time of need. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jer 11:15</reference> is very obscure; and from the Masoretic text it is hardly possible to obtain a suitable sense. "The beloved" of Jahveh is Judah, the covenant people; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">Deu 33:12</reference>, where Benjamin is so called, and <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jer 12:7</reference>, where the Lord calls His people ידידוּת נפשׁי. "What is to my beloved in my house?" i.e., what has my people to do in my house - what does it want there? "My house" is the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, as appears from the mention of holy flesh in the second clause. The main difficulty lies in the words עשׂותהּ המזמּתה הרבּים. Hitz. takes עשׂותהּ to be the subject of the clause, and makes the suffix point back to ידידי, which, as collective, is to be construed <hi type="italic">generis faem</hi>.: what should the accomplishment of his plans be to my beloved in my house? But as adverse to this we must note, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. the improbability of ידיד as used of the people being feminine; <hi type="italic">b</hi>. the fact that even if we adopt Hitz.'s change of המזמּתה into המזמּות, yet the latter word does not mean plans or designs to bring offerings. The phrase is clearly to be taken by itself as a continuation of the question; and the suffix to be regarded, with Ew., Umbr., etc., as pointing, in the Aramaic fashion, to the object following: they who practise guile. מזמּה, a thinking out, devising, usually of hurtful schemes, here guile, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">Psa 139:20</reference>; Job 21:27. What is meant is the hypocrisy of cloaking their apostasy from God by offering sacrifices in the temple, of concealing their idolatry and passing themselves off as worshippers of Jahve. On the form מזמּתה, see Ew. §173, <hi type="italic">g</hi>, Gesen. §80, Rem. 2,f. הרבּים makes no sense. It belongs manifestly to the words which follow; for it can neither be subject to עשׂותהּ, nor can it be joined to המזמּתה as its genitive. The lxx render: μὴ εὐχαὶ καὶ κρέα ἅγια ἀφελοῦσιν ἀπὸ σοῦ τὰς κακίας σου; and following this, Dathe, Dahl., Ew., Hitz. hold הנדרים to be the original reading. On the other hand, Maur., Graf, and Näg. think we should read הרנּים (after <reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">Psa 32:7</reference>) or הרנּים myinirah, crying, loud supplication; on the ground of Buxtorf’s hint, <hi type="italic">Anticrit</hi>. p. 661, that probably the Alexandrians had הרבּים in their text, but, changing the ב for נ, read הרנים. We must make our choice between these two conjectures; for even if הרבּים did not stand in the codex used by the Alexandrians, it cannot have been the original word.
